title: Why Alella tastes the way it does

lede.text: Alella's vines grow on sauló, the small grains that granite breaks into at the surface, and it drains so well that the vine has to root deep for water. The white wines show fruit and fresh mineral notes, and they end on a bitter, citrus finish.

chapters.title: A city's vineyard between sea and mountain
paras: Alella lies north of Barcelona and covers about 320 hectares. It is one of the smallest and oldest appellations on the Iberian Peninsula. Two comarcas, or districts, share it. The Maresme lies by the sea, and the Vallès Oriental lies on the far side of the Cordillera Litoral, the coastal range.
The vines have fought for survival against the growing city for many years. Pliny and Martial already cited these wines in Roman times, as Laietanian wines.

fly.caption: A small vineyard north of Barcelona, split between the sea side and the inland side of the coastal range.

fly.caption: The Montseny park, in the Vallès Oriental, was declared a biosphere reserve in 1978.

chapters.title: Sea breeze through the passes
paras: The Maresme has a Mediterranean coastal climate. Autumn is the rainy season and summer the dry one. Average rain ranges from 550 mm to 800 mm a year. Summers are hot, with averages of 22 °C to 23 °C, and winters are mild, averaging 8 °C to 10 °C. Frost can come only from November to March.

On the sea side, the Cordillera Litoral shelters a corridor from cold inland winds and holds in the marinada, the sea breeze. It does so especially in summer, when temperatures there are usually quite high.

Inland, the Vallès Oriental has a Mediterranean climate that varies with the lie of the land. Rain is irregular, from 1200 mm down to 600 mm a year, and the total is scarce except on the highest ground. Frost-free weather lasts only five months, from May to September. Morning mist is caught by the western slope of the range. In summer the marinada cools the vines as it comes through three natural passes between the two sides. One is the Coll de Parpes, and the others are Font de Cera and La Conreria.
Inland wines show a little more acidity than those from the sea side.

fly.caption: The sea side of the range: a sheltered corridor that holds in the summer sea breeze.

chapters.title: Granite that turns to sand
paras: The Cordillera Litoral is granite. In a mild climate, air and water break it down into rounded rocks and then into sauló. Storms have washed sauló down to the low ground, where it forms the coastal farmland.

Most Maresme vineyard soils are built on sauló. It is not very fertile. The soil is sandy and light in colour, almost white. It is airy and drains well, but it holds little water or nutrients. It also retains the sun's radiation well and is slightly alkaline. Water does not pool, even in heavy storms, which matters for the health of the roots.
Under the surface, the granite carries marine remains. Having to root deep puts the vine under a little stress that, well managed, helps regulate the yield per vine.

chapters.title: Pansa Blanca, Garnacha and a long list of styles
paras: Most white wine is made from Pansa Blanca, the main white grape here. Pansa Blanca and Garnacha Blanca are the preferred whites, and Moscatel is also recommended. The recommended red is Garnacha tinta, and most red wine is made from it. Many others are grown, Chardonnay and Syrah among them.

Whites can be made in stainless steel, with skin contact, or fermented and aged in barrel. Stainless steel gives fresh apple and very ripe pear. Barrel ageing gives baked apple. Skin contact gives a bright yellow colour with peach and apricot. The bitter, citrus finish recalls green almond. Barrel-aged reds from Garnacha tinta smell of cherry jam and cocoa, with liquorice and toast as well, depending on how long they age. Young reds from stainless steel smell of very ripe cherry and Maresme strawberry. Both end bitter and mineral, recalling black plum. Rosados smell of red fruit. In the mouth they are fresh, yet mellow and powerful.

Alella also makes sparkling wine by the traditional method, with a second fermentation in the bottle. It can be white, rosado or blanc de noirs. Sparkling wine ages nine months, counted from the tirage, the bottling for the second fermentation, to disgorging. Vino de aguja, a lightly sparkling wine, keeps part of the carbon dioxide from its own fermentation.

It also makes liqueur wines. Rancio comes from Garnacha Blanca and Macabeo or from Garnacha tinta. It ages exposed to air, out in the sun by day and the night air, called sol y serena, and spends at least a year in oak. Rancio sold as crianza needs four years of ageing, at least three of them in oak. Grape spirit may be added if needed. Its colour is old gold, and it ends on mineral, marine, salty notes. Mistela is fortified. It is made from the free-run must of white grapes, mostly Pansa Blanca. The wine is filtered at 12% natural alcohol or more, and then grape spirit is added. Vino dulce natural comes from must with more than 250 g/l of sugar, partly fermented. All three hold 15% to 20% alcohol by volume.
Yields are capped at 12,000 kg of grapes per hectare for white varieties and 10,000 kg for red.

terms.text: Red wine ages 24 months with at least 6 months in oak barrel. White and rosado wines age at least 18 months, also with at least 6 months in oak. For Crianza, Reserva and Gran reserva the oak barrels hold at most 1,000 litres.

Red wine ages at least 36 months, with at least 12 months in oak barrel and 24 months in bottle. White and rosado wines age at least 24 months, with at least 6 months in barrel and 18 months in bottle.
Red wine spends at least 24 months in oak barrel and 36 months in bottle. White and rosado wines age at least 48 months, with at least 6 months in oak and 42 months in bottle.
The word barrica, barrel, may appear when the label gives the time in months and years and the type of wooden container, which can hold at most 600 litres.
The word roble, oak, may appear when the label gives the months or years the wine spent in oak containers of at most 330 litres.
Fermented in oak barrel. It may appear when the wine fermented in wooden containers of at most 600 litres.
New wine. It is sold only with the vintage on the label, and it is bottled during the season and/or from 11 November of the harvest year.
Young wine. It is sold only with the vintage on the label, and it is bottled during the season and/or from 20 December of the harvest year.
Seco, dry, has at most 4 g/l of sugar. Semiseco has more than 4 g/l and up to 12 g/l. Semidulce has more than 12 g/l and up to 45 g/l. Dulce, sweet, has more than 45 g/l.
One variety may be named if it makes up 85% or more of the wine. Up to three may be named if the wine is made only from them, in decreasing order of their share.
The harvest year may be named if 85% or more of the grapes come from that year.
